A mobile radio runs from a vehicle electrical system, about 13.8 volts. That rules out the two 24-volt choices.
Now find the power each 13.8-volt supply can deliver. Cover P on the triangle: I and E are left side by side, so multiply.
The 4-ampere supply gives barely more than the 50 watts going out. A transmitter also loses power as heat, so this is too small.
The 12-ampere supply gives plenty for 50 watts out plus the heat.

Decibels compare two powers, so find the ratio first: end power divided by start power.
The power doubled. On the ladder, doubling is one step of +3 dB.

One quarter is two halvings in a row.
On the ladder each halving is -3 dB. Decibels add up, and the minus sign means the power went down.

The power is ten times bigger. On the ladder, ten times is one step of +10 dB.
Radio waves travel at about 300,000,000 meters per second. Wavelength is that speed divided by the frequency.
Megahertz means millions of hertz. The millions cancel, so only 300 is left on top.
Test it on a band you know. 146 MHz should come out near 2 meters, and it does.

answer: Wavelength in meters equals 300 divided by frequency in megahertz

A battery is rated in ampere-hours. That means amperes multiplied by hours.
Divide the rating by the amperes your equipment draws on average. The amperes cancel and only hours are left.
Practice example with made-up numbers: a 10 ampere-hour battery feeding an average of 2 amperes.

answer: Divide the battery ampere-hour rating by the average current draw of the equipment

steps.say: Duty cycle is the percentage of time the transmitter is on. Here it falls to half.
RF exposure limits apply to the average over time. On for half the time means half the average exposure.
So the level allowed while transmitting can go up by the inverse.

answer: It increases by a factor of 2
